## Chapter 19

Chaos (1870)

One fine May afternoon in 1870 he drove again up St. James’s Street, wondering at the marvels of life. Outwardly London was the same; outwardly Europe showed no great change. Reform ran riot; Evolution from lower to higher raged like an epidemic; Darwin was the prophet of the most evolutionary of worlds. Improvement, prosperity, power, seemed to leap and bound over every country road. Even America, with her scandals and Claims, hardly jarred.

In society the long Adams reign at the Legation was forgotten; a new “smart set” had come to its own; houses once familiar were closing; death had ravaged the older circle. Experience ceased to educate. He found himself more eighteenth-century than ever—almost rococo—and could not catch the cog-wheels of evolution. English reforms he cared nothing for; they were themselves mediæval. He resented change. He would have kept the Pope in the Vatican and the Queen at Windsor Castle as historical monuments. The tourist was the great conservative who hated novelty and adored dirt. He came back for amusement, quiet, gaiety; not for revolution.

Common-sense bade him make court to Marlborough House with the American woman and the Jew banker; but, by some law of Anglo-Saxon atrophy, he and his friends were unfashionable. He had no thought that within three months his world would be upset and he under it. Frank Palgrave, contentious as ever, said that “Germany would beat France into scraps” if there were war; Adams thought not. The chances were always against catastrophes.

London first played lightly with him. He sniffed with voluptuous delight the coal-smoke of Cheapside, revelled in the architecture of Oxford Street; May Fair never shone so fair; he loved it all—everything—had always loved it; he thought he owned the St. James’s Club. Then Nature struck with a brutal hand, and the last lesson—the sum and term of education—began.

Editors refused his Gold Conspiracy article, not for style but for fear. One could set down such timidity to respectability and law, but to find an English Quarterly scared into silence by Gould and Fisk passed even his large experience of English eccentricity. He sent the paper on to a Radical review and left it.

A telegram called him to the Bagni di Lucca: his sister had been thrown from a cab. He reached her when tetanus had already set in. Hour by hour the muscles grew rigid while the mind remained bright, and after ten days of fiendish torture she died in convulsion. He had heard much of death and seen a little, and knew by heart the commonplaces that deaden sense; but he had never seen Nature—only her surface—the sugar-coating that she shows to youth. The terror of the blow stayed by him thenceforth. Nature enjoyed it, played with it; the horror added to her charm; she liked the torture and smothered her victim with caresses. The Italian summer brooded; the hills seemed bursting with mid-summer blood; even the dying woman shared the courage and sensual fulness of the air. For thousands of years on these hills and plains Nature had gone on sabring men and women with the same air of pleasure.

The first serious consciousness of Nature’s gesture—her attitude towards life—took form as a phantasm, a nightmare, an insanity of force. The stage-scenery of the senses collapsed; the mind felt itself stripped naked in a void of shapeless energies, colliding, crushing, wasting, destroying what they had labored from eternity to perfect. The anodynes of social medicine showed as artifice. Stoicism was perhaps best; religion the most human; but that any personal deity could find pleasure or profit in torturing a poor woman, by accident, with a cruelty known to man only in perverted temperaments, could not be held for a moment. For pure blasphemy, it made pure atheism a comfort. God might be, as the Church said, a Substance, but He could not be a Person.

He crept northward to Ouchy to recover balance in a new world. For the first time Mont Blanc looked to him what it was—a chaos of anarchic and purposeless forces—until days of repose helped it clothe itself again with the illusions of the senses: white purity, splendor of light, heavenly peace. Nature was kind; but before her illusions were quite restored, Europe’s vanished. On July 4 all Europe was in peace; on July 14 it was in full chaos of war. In Paris, war came out like an opera of Meyerbeer; patriotism was served by order in grammes per capita; regiment after regiment marched shouting the Marseillaise while the bystanders hardly cared to join. He fled to England and the profound peace of Wenlock Abbey, where the August sun lay warm, the rookery cawed at sunset, and since the reign of Pteraspis nothing had greatly changed—nothing except the monks who now read war-correspondence on the turf.

A letter invited him to take an Assistant Professorship of History at Harvard. He thanked the new President and declined; he knew nothing of history and less of teaching. He sailed from Liverpool on September 1, to begin again as a free lance. Yet home brought queer rewards. His article on the Session in the July North American had been reprinted by the Democratic Committee and circulated by the hundred thousand; at once he was in opposition, and a Massachusetts Democrat. The London paper on the Gold Conspiracy followed, pirated on a great scale. A Senator, answering him in a campaign document, besides refuting his opinions, did him the honor—most picturesque in senatorial rhetoric—of likening him to a begonia: curious, showy foliage; conspicuous; insisting on the most prominent positions; useful perhaps to a gardener, not to the Treasury.

No sooner had he made at Washington what he modestly hoped was a success than his family set on him to drag him away. His father interposed; his mother entreated; his brother urged Cambridge. The professorship was to be coupled with the North American Review; it would give him weight; he needed the university more than it needed him. He went to see the President. “But, Mr. President,” he urged, “I know nothing about Mediæval History.” With courteous manner and bland smile the answer came: “If you will point out to me any one who knows more, Mr. Adams, I will appoint him.” Not logical, but not to be met within his privileges. At twenty-four hours’ notice he broke life in halves again to begin a new education, on lines he had not chosen, in subjects for which he cared less than nothing; in a place he did not love, before a future that repelled.

Grant’s administration wrecked men by thousands and profited few; the period was poor in purpose and barren in results. Why then should Washington be held more fatal than New York? All respectable America agreed that Washington was no place for a respectable young man; all Washington agreed and conspired to drive every young man away. Not one of promise remained in the service. Government did not want them. Yet Harvard, which he had persistently criticised, alone offered him an office, a dollar, an encouragement, a kindness. Measured by money and patronage, the college Government was a matter of more importance than some branches of the national service, and in social position superior to them all. If Harvard thought him worth employing at four dollars a day, why should Washington decline his services when he asked nothing?

The American character, as he read it there, showed singular limitations. At Washington the American was four times in five a quiet, peaceful, shy figure, like Lincoln—somewhat sad; or like Grant—inarticulate, uncertain, distrustful of himself and of others, awed by money. Work and whiskey were his stimulants; work a form of vice; he had no use for wealth after he earned it; the amusement of pursuit was all the amusement he got. Bored, patient, helpless; dependent on wife and daughters; indulgent; modest and decent; valuable citizens, they thronged Europe’s stations, carefully explaining that the happiest day would be the day they landed at New York. They were ashamed to be amused; their minds no longer answered to variety; they could not face a new thought. Congress was full of such men; in the Executive the same; they knew not how to amuse themselves, nor conceive how others were amused. Work, whiskey, and cards were life. If the outside world judged that Washington was fatal even for a young man of thirty-two who never played cards and loathed whiskey, it was because the atmosphere belonged to them, or was supposed to be in their control.

Thus his summer that promised only amusement ended in intimate tragedy and a terrific political convulsion; he failed of every errand he had set—Quarterlies refusing his best essay; no new acquaintances taken up; but he found himself carried by family pressure and college invitation into a new harness. Education had brought him to the cross-roads where all led astray; he chose the one that at least offered him a desk.

## Chapter 20

Failure (1871)

He had, as a child, seen the old President’s House on Harvard Square when his aunt kept its colonial self-respect; now the drawing-room and deserted kitchen stood to let, and he took them for his quarters. Above, his brother had rooms; opposite, a young instructor; there was a boarding-table where men of learning gathered. Primitive arrangements satisfied them, and the Assistant Professor had no time to waste; for nine months he exhausted his strength trying to keep a day ahead of duty.

Between Gurney’s classical courses and Torrey’s modern ones lay a gap of a thousand years which Adams must fill. Students had already elected the unknown courses. Down to the moment he faced them, he had given, as far as he remembered, an hour, more or less, to the Middle Ages. Not that his ignorance troubled him; he knew enough to be ignorant. Yet education is a serious thing. A parent gives life, but as parent, gives no more. A murderer takes life, but his deed stops there. A teacher affects eternity; he can never tell where his influence stops.

A teacher must either treat history as a catalogue, a record, a romance, or as an evolution; and whether he affirms or denies evolution, he falls into the burning faggots of the pit. He makes of his scholars either priests or atheists, plutocrats or socialists, judges or anarchists, almost in spite of himself. Adams had no theory to teach and could not make the facts fit one. He would not amuse sluggish-minded boys with agreeable tales; still less compel them to learn the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle and the Venerable Bede by heart. He saw no relation between his students and the Middle Ages except the Church—and there the ground was dangerous. Since Gibbon, history had nowhere broken down so pitiably as there; it was a hundred years behind the experimental sciences.

He could use Maine, Tylor, McLennan, Buckle, Comte, and the rest, but could fit them into no theory of his own. Half his time the College expected him to drill dates enough to save their degrees from disgrace. This was formal; he told the boys they might get their facts where they liked, and use the teacher for questions; the one privilege worth claiming was talk with the professor, and he strove to force them to risk criticism from their fellows. Any large body of students stifles the student. No man can instruct more than half-a-dozen at once. The lecture system of hundreds—very much that of the twelfth century—suited him not at all.

He would try to cultivate the tenth mind that sensibly reacts, though at the expense of the other nine. Since no text-books existed, he refused to profess, and joined the best workers in trying to find the best way of learning. They read what they pleased and compared results—historical method. The boys worked like rabbits, digging holes all over archaic society; unknown languages yielded; customary law became familiar; they learned to chase an idea like a hare through thickets of obscure fact. As pedagogy, triumphant; as preparation, useless. The science had no system; its subject was antiquarian; he could not make it actual. He needed conflict, competition, contradiction; he would have seated a rival assistant opposite him to express the opposite view; nothing else would interest teacher or taught; but of all university freaks, none shocked the air so much as competition between teachers. In that respect the thirteenth-century university was worth the modern school.

Despite President Eliot’s reforms and steady, generous support, the system remained costly, clumsy, futile; the university—as far as it was represented by Henry Adams—produced, at great waste, results not worth reaching. Fashion came to help him torture his students with Germany: Pepins and Merwigs, Othos and Barbarossas; Bryce’s Holy Roman Empire; the new Emperor at Versailles. He imposed Germany with a heavy hand. He was rejoiced; but doubted they should be grateful. On the whole, neither what he taught nor how he taught it contented him. The seven years seemed to him lost.

He quitted the university in 1877 with the feeling that, but for the invariable courtesy and kindness shown him from President to injured students, he should be sore at his failure. The college expressed the opposite view; kindness went so far that the President hinted his services merited recognition. He could have wept for gratitude, but could not let the college suppose him entitled to distinction. He esteemed himself a respectable failure; yet nothing struck him more than that Harvard, which he had criticised, abused, abandoned, neglected, should alone offer him office, dollar, encouragement, kindness. Harvard might have faults, but it redeemed America by being true to its own.

If anything succeeded, it was the students. Without violent emotion or sentiment, ignorant of all that man had ever thought or hoped except for the veneer of American habit, their minds burst open at the sunlight of suggestion; quick to respond, plastic to a mould, incapable of fatigue. Their faith in education was full of pathos. When he asked what they could do with it, one answered: “The degree of Harvard College is worth money to me in Chicago.” The reply upset his experience, for the degree had been a drawback in Boston and Washington; but so far as it went, it was good, and settled one’s doubts. He had given twenty years to the same pursuit and was no nearer a result than they; he still had to take for granted that his teaching did them more good than harm. In his own opinion, the greatest good he could do them was to hold his tongue.

Unlike himself, his colleagues knew their business. The Professor of Chemistry cared not a chemical atom whether society was virtuous; the Professor of Physics smiled at evolution; the Political Economist treated the triumphs of the Church’s art as waste of force. They knew what they had to teach; he did not. He could teach his students nothing; he was only educating himself at their cost.
